title: Tech-savvy adult with advanced connectivity needs

patient.chiefConcern: Difficulty hearing speech in restaurants and frequent smartphone use

featurePrompt: Which clinical and lifestyle features should influence the hearing-aid plan?

keyFeatures.label: Lifestyle
keyFeatures.value: Frequent smartphone use and active social listening

summary: C1 tests integration of audiometry, listening demands and technology preferences rather than choosing features in isolation.

stages.title: 1. Synthesize the patient's needs
stages.prompt: Which factor should guide the technology discussion?

options.text: Restaurant speech-in-noise demands, smartphone use and the patient's priorities
Only the degree of hearing loss
The newest available hearing aid regardless of use case

stages.feedback: Needs assessment should connect the hearing profile with real-world listening and device-use goals.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the hearing profile
stages.prompt: How should the audiogram influence selection?

options.text: Use the configuration to establish an appropriate fitting target while considering the patient's listening demands
Let the hearing aid model determine the interpretation
Ignore the configuration because connectivity is the main goal

stages.feedback: Technology selection follows clinical fitting requirements; connectivity is an additional patient-centred consideration.

stages.title: 3. Check practical constraints
stages.prompt: What should be confirmed before finalizing the feature set?

options.text: Phone compatibility, dexterity, expectations, listening environments and willingness to use the features
Only the colour of the device
Assume all phones and devices connect identically

stages.feedback: Connectivity features are useful only when they fit the patient's actual devices and routine.

stages.title: 4. Select and fit the technology
stages.prompt: Which plan best matches the case?

options.text: Appropriate acoustic fitting with speech-in-noise features plus compatible wireless streaming/connectivity options
Choose connectivity first and adjust acoustics later
Avoid all automatic processing because the patient uses a smartphone

stages.feedback: The plan should integrate acoustic fitting with the patient's communication and connectivity needs.

stages.title: 5. Justify verification and counselling
stages.prompt: What should the rationale include?

options.text: Explain how fitting/verification confirms appropriate amplification and how selected features address the patient's environments
State that premium features guarantee benefit
Skip verification because the patient is technology confident

stages.feedback: Verification and counselling remain important even when a patient is comfortable with technology.

stages.title: 6. Plan follow-up
stages.prompt: Which outcomes should be reviewed?

options.text: Speech-in-noise benefit, daily use, streaming reliability, comfort and patient-reported satisfaction
Only whether Bluetooth appears connected
Only aided thresholds

stages.feedback: Follow-up should measure functional benefit and whether the technology works in the patient's actual routine.

title: Precipitous high-frequency hearing loss with open-fit considerations

patient.chiefConcern: Difficulty understanding speech despite hearing high-frequency sounds as loud enough

featurePrompt: Which features are most important when translating this configuration into a fitting decision?

keyFeatures.label: Listening issue
keyFeatures.value: Speech clarity remains limited despite amplification

keyFeatures.label: Acoustic question
keyFeatures.value: Open-fit versus alternative coupling and frequency-specific strategy

summary: C2 is designed to make students connect the audiometric configuration, acoustic coupling and the limits of amplification when speech clarity remains difficult.

stages.title: 1. Synthesize the listening problem
stages.prompt: What should be clarified?

options.text: Speech clarity difficulty, listening environments, current fitting experience and expectations
Only the patient's preferred colour
Assume more high-frequency gain will always solve clarity

stages.feedback: The patient's experience with clarity and the current fitting should guide further reasoning.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the configuration
stages.prompt: What is clinically important about the precipitous high-frequency loss?

options.text: The steep configuration creates acoustic and amplification considerations that must be balanced with usable low-frequency hearing
It is equivalent to a flat moderate loss for fitting purposes
Only the better low frequencies matter

stages.feedback: A precipitous configuration requires careful consideration of coupling and frequency-specific amplification.

stages.title: 3. Check fitting constraints
stages.prompt: What should be evaluated before changing the fitting?

options.text: Occlusion, feedback risk, available high-frequency audibility, speech understanding and the patient's tolerance
Only maximum output
No need for verification

stages.feedback: The fitting should be evaluated across acoustic comfort, audibility and functional benefit.

stages.title: 4. Select the fitting approach
stages.prompt: Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Select coupling and amplification based on the configuration, verify the fitting and consider an alternative strategy if conventional high-frequency gain is not useful
Maximize high-frequency gain without verification
Use an open fit in every precipitous loss

stages.feedback: Open fitting can be considered in appropriate configurations, but the decision should be individualized and verified.

stages.title: 5. Justify the fitting
stages.prompt: Which rationale is strongest?

options.text: The fitting strategy is chosen to balance the patient's usable low-frequency hearing, high-frequency needs, comfort and measurable benefit
The fitting is correct because it is a standard preset
Any hearing aid can provide equivalent speech clarity

stages.feedback: A defensible rationale connects the acoustic decision to the patient's configuration and outcomes.

stages.title: 6. Plan outcome measurement
stages.prompt: What should be reviewed after fitting changes?

options.text: Speech understanding, sound quality, comfort, aided audibility and patient-reported benefit
Only battery life
Only unaided thresholds

stages.feedback: Outcome measures should determine whether the fitting change actually improves function.

title: Severe hearing loss with dexterity and visual limitations

patient.chiefConcern: Difficulty handling small hearing-aid controls and seeing device indicators

featurePrompt: Which patient factors should influence device and fitting decisions?

keyFeatures.label: Hearing need
keyFeatures.value: Severe hearing loss requiring substantial amplification

keyFeatures.label: Additional barrier
keyFeatures.value: Poor visual acuity affecting small controls and indicators

summary: C3 tests whether hearing-aid selection accounts for handling and visual usability in addition to the audiogram and amplification requirements.

stages.title: 1. Synthesize the patient profile
stages.prompt: What must be included in needs assessment?

options.text: Amplification needs, dexterity, visual ability, daily support and device-management routine
Only the audiogram
Only cosmetic preference

stages.feedback: Usability and independent management are central to this patient's hearing-aid needs.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the hearing profile
stages.prompt: How should the severe loss influence selection?

options.text: It establishes substantial amplification requirements that must be combined with an appropriate physical design and coupling
It means any device style is equally suitable
It removes the need for verification

stages.feedback: The hearing profile guides amplification, while physical usability guides device design.

stages.title: 3. Screen for usability barriers
stages.prompt: What should be addressed before finalizing the device?

options.text: Battery/charging handling, controls, visual indicators, retention, caregiver support and communication needs
Assume the patient can manipulate all small controls
Ignore support needs

stages.feedback: The case specifically highlights dexterity and visual limitations as design constraints.

stages.title: 4. Select the fitting and device approach
stages.prompt: Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Choose an appropriately powerful, secure and easy-to-handle design with simplified controls and support/training as needed
Choose the smallest possible device regardless of usability
Avoid hearing aids because the patient is older

stages.feedback: Device selection should balance amplification, physical usability and support.

stages.title: 5. Justify counselling and verification
stages.prompt: What should the rationale include?

options.text: Verification of the fitting plus hands-on counselling adapted to the patient's visual and motor abilities
A standard written instruction sheet alone
No counselling is needed if the device is programmed correctly

stages.feedback: Programming is only part of successful hearing-aid management; training must match patient abilities.

stages.title: 6. Plan follow-up
stages.prompt: What should be checked after fitting?

options.text: Comfort, handling, daily use, caregiver support, communication benefit and any physical problems with the device
Only the visual appearance
Only the audiogram

stages.feedback: Follow-up should identify barriers that appear only during real-world device use.

title: Returning user with feedback, occlusion and unnatural voice perception

patient.chiefConcern: Hearing aid whistles and own voice sounds unnatural

featurePrompt: Which complaint pattern should be separated into distinct troubleshooting problems?

keyFeatures.label: Clinical task
keyFeatures.value: Separate acoustic causes before changing gain or replacing the device

summary: C4 is a troubleshooting case. Students should distinguish feedback from occlusion and avoid changing multiple fitting variables without first identifying the likely cause.

stages.title: 1. Clarify the complaints
stages.prompt: What is the best first step?

options.text: Characterize when whistling occurs and separately characterize the own-voice/occlusion complaint
Increase gain immediately
Assume the hearing aid is defective

stages.feedback: Separating the complaints helps avoid treating different acoustic problems as one issue.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the troubleshooting pattern
stages.prompt: Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Whistling suggests a feedback pathway, while own-voice complaints may require assessment of coupling, venting and low-frequency amplification
Both complaints prove the receiver is broken
All complaints should be treated by increasing gain

stages.feedback: The two complaints can have different acoustic mechanisms and should be investigated separately.

stages.title: 3. Check simple causes first
stages.prompt: What should be checked before major programming changes?

options.text: Physical fit, earwax/obstruction, tubing or receiver seating, venting and feedback-management settings
Replace the device without inspection
Ignore the physical fit

stages.feedback: Troubleshooting should begin with straightforward physical and coupling checks.

stages.title: 4. Select troubleshooting actions
stages.prompt: Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Correct the identified physical/acoustic cause, then make targeted programming changes and verify the result
Increase all frequencies until the whistle stops
Turn off all processing without assessing the cause

stages.feedback: Targeted troubleshooting is preferable to broad, unexplained programming changes.

stages.title: 5. Justify the intervention
stages.prompt: Which rationale demonstrates good troubleshooting?

options.text: Each change is linked to a specific complaint mechanism and checked for effect before moving to the next adjustment
The most aggressive programming change is most efficient
Patient complaints are less useful than the default fitting

stages.feedback: A defensible troubleshooting chain links complaint, suspected mechanism, targeted action and outcome.

stages.title: 6. Plan follow-up
stages.prompt: What should be documented after the adjustment?

options.text: Whether whistling and own-voice perception improved, comfort, use and any recurrence triggers
Only whether the device powers on
No follow-up is required after a programming change

stages.feedback: Follow-up confirms whether the troubleshooting actually solved the patient's functional complaint.
